speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: FEED GRAINS-ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN SUBSIDY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before motions are proceeded with I should like to make an announcement with regard to the freight assistance on western feed grains.
The present freight assistance policy establishes four main receiving zones, three in eastern Canada and one in British Columbia. The rate of assistance is calculated on a different formula for each zone. In eastern Canada it is arranged so that the ratio of assistance to freight costs increases as the zones move east.
Zone 1 is old Ontario and western Quebec, in which all points have a common rail freight rate from the lakehead, known as the Montreal freight rate zone. Zone 2 is eastern Quebec beyond the Montreal zone, except the Gaspe. Zone 3 is the Atlantic provinces and the Gaspe. Zone 4 is British Columbia.
The present assistance rates are now fixed in relation to the freight rates prevailing on January 26, 1955, the date of the order. As a result of the recent freight rate increase the assistance bears a lower relation to freight costs than formerly. The comparison, for typical points in each zone, is as follows:

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR LIST OF BOOKS REFUSED ENTRY INTO CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday in answer to a question by the hon. member for Peel I undertook to consider his request that I table in the house the number and titles of books prohibited entry into Canada during the last year. The number of such books was 79.
As to my tabling the titles of those publications, I should like to remind the hon. member and the house that when similar requests have been made in the past the house has appreciated the fact that it has been the continued policy of successive governments to not make public the titles of books classified as immoral, indecent or seditious under tariff item 1201, which has been in the tariff since confederation. It has apparently been felt that the government should not be the supplier of a list of selected books of this character. Furthermore, the publication of such titles could serve as a catalogue for persons interested in the clandestine importation, distribution or sale of this kind of literature.
As I have previously explained in the house, when a publication is classified under this item the importer, exporter and publisher are advised of its classification and of their right of appeal to the tariff board or to the exchequer court. As in the past, I would say to the hon. member for Peel that

Inquiries of the Ministry I would be glad to make the list of titles available to him for such use as he may see fit.
With this explanation I would hope the hon. gentleman would agree that it would not be in the public interest to have the list tabled.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY AIRLIFT FACILITIES FROM UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I promised the other day that as soon as I was able to do so I would make a short statement about the proposed airlift for British and French immigrants. Of course in practice the airlift will largely be for British immigrants because, unfortunately, we do not seem to be able to induce very many Frenchmen to come to Canada, a condition I regret.
The Department of Citizenship and Immigration recently approached the intergovernmental committee for European migration, of which Canada is a member, with a view to arranging for the charter of 350 air flights to transport immigrants to Canada from the United Kingdom and France. Implementation of the details of this arrangement is subject,

Inquiries of the Ministry
of course, to the approval of the Canadian air transport board, which is now considering this matter. However, it has been approved in principle, and the first flight will be made about March 15. The reason I am making the announcement today is so the ticketing and other arrangements can be proceeded with.
This is the largest airlift ever undertaken by the Canadian government, at least of this character, and it will be known as "Air Bridge to Canada" or "A.B.C.". That is to make it simpler for everybody to remember. The airlift is designed to add to regular commercial air and steamship transportation which is, or looks like being, booked to capacity during the early spring and summer months. It will provide for the transportation of immigrants who could not otherwise be moved in that period.
It is intended that the flight schedule of "Air Bridge to Canada" will be as follows- and I have a table here, Mr. Speaker, showing where these flights will go. Perhaps I need not read it now, but have permission to insert it in Hansard.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to ask a question of the Minister of Trade and Commerce arising out of certain items that have appeared in the United States press in recent days and today appear in our press, relative to an alleged practice on the part of Canadian flour millers of filling their export orders in part by having United States millers mill United States wheat, put it in Canadian bags, and thereby in part fill Canadian export market requirements. Is there any foundation for the statements as to this practice? If so, to what extent is the practice being continued, and is it this practice that has brought about the condition of affairs whereby our flour exports are decreasing while our exports of wheat are increasing?

maintopic: REPORTED EXPORT OF U.S. FLOUR UNDER CANADIAN BRAND NAMES

I do not think it would be good policy to go into the reasons for the practice, but we are taking steps which we think will make that policy less attractive. I do not think it is carried on to a great extent but there is a situation affecting exports of flour, particularly to certain flour markets, which requires correction. The correction is being made, and I hope to make an announcement in a day or two.

maintopic: REPORTED EXPORT OF U.S. FLOUR UNDER CANADIAN BRAND NAMES
speechtext:

would say whether or not this has been a general practice. speechtext: Will the minister say whether or not-

maintopic: APPLICATION TO SHARES PURCHASED UNDER OPTIONS BY EMPLOYEES

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, February 27, consideration in committee of Bill No. 46, to amend the Export Credits Insurance Act-Mr. Howe (Port Arthur)-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
On clause 2-Deduction, for income tax, of credits to underwriting reserve.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose yesterday the hon. member for

Eglinton and the hon. member for Greenwood had been raising some questions in connection with the setting up of the underwriting reserve of this company, and the provisions of the section in the amending bill which will extend to the corporation the privilege of deducting for income tax purposes the amounts credited to this underwriting reserve until the reserve reaches the statutory maximum of $5 million.
I had explained to the committee that the purpose of this amendment was to place this corporation in a similar position in connection with the payment of income tax on the amounts credited to the reserve fund to that in which privately owned insurance companies are under the legislation applicable to them. In order to make this position clear I would refer hon. members to section 12 (1) (e) of the Income Tax Act, which reads:
(e) an amount transferred or credited to a reserve, contingent account or sinking fund except as expressly permitted by this part.
In other words that section prevents companies from deducting for income tax purposes amounts transferred to reserve or contingent accounts except as expressly permitted. The relevant permission as set out in the act will be found in section 85B (5) which reads:
Paragraph (c) of subsection (1) does not apply to allow a deduction as a reserve in respect of insurance, but an insurance corporation, other than a life insurance corporation, may, in computing its income from its insurance business for a taxation year, deduct as policy reserves such amounts as have been approved for the purposes of this subsection by the superintendent of insurance.
The exemption contained in the Income Tax Act permits the superintendent of insurance to approve policy reserves in such amounts as he may fix, and those are accepted by the Department of National Revenue as deductions from the income of that insurance company for the year for income tax purposes. The superintendent of insurance occupies a position created by the Department of Insurance Act, and his jurisdiction extends only to those companies which come under the act. The Export Credits Insurance Corporation, which is the corporation with which we are concerned in this bill, does not fall within that category and accordingly cannot enjoy the exemptions provided for other insurance companies by the insurance act in so far as approved reserves are concerned.
I am also informed that even if the superintendent of insurance were to feel himself justified, although this corporation does not come under the Department of Insurance Act, to give advice as to the reserves, the fact is that the superintendent of insurance

would not be in a position to give that advice because the business of this corporation does not lend itself to actuarial calculation in the way an ordinary insurance business does, and it would not be practicable to suggest that the superintendent have this particular authority in connection with this corporation.
I am sure all hon. members would agree that this insurance corporation must and should have reserves to provide for possible future losses which cannot be foreseen, and if it were to be required to pay income tax on the present basis I am informed that it would have to increase the rates of premium to cover the payment of income tax and enable it, at the same time, to build up its reserve; and that this would involve a substantially heavier charge upon exporters and would make the insurance available through the corporation non-competitive as compared with the type of insurance which is available to competing exporters in foreign countries. If an increase in premium rates were to be required for this purpose our coverage with regard to Canadian exports would be noncompetitive and would in many cases be found to be too high for Canadian exporters.
The information I have, Mr. Chairman, is that similar government owned and operated insurance corporations in other countries do not pay income tax, but so far as this corporation is concerned it is not trying to avoid the payment of income tax, or the application of the general policy which has been adopted for crown corporations as was indicated in the debate in the committee yesterday afternoon. However, by this amendment it would be placed in a position where it could accumulate a statutory reserve to cover future unknown losses without paying income tax on the amounts put into that reserve, in the same way ordinary insurance companies are permitted to build up their reserves with the approval of the superintendent of insurance for exactly the same purpose without paying income tax on those credits.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when this matter came up yesterday we recalled to the parliamentary assistant the statement made by the Minister of Finance in 1952 with regard to crown corporations paying their income tax like other people. At that time the parliamentary assistant said something which, I confess, shook us a bit. He said at page 1722 of Hansard for yesterday:
Under the Income Tax Act, the fact is that all private insurance companies are entitled to set up reserves free of income tax. The purpose and effect of this clause is simply to extend the same privilege to this company which, under the wording of the Income Tax Act, is not entitled to the privilege which is extended to other insurance companies. It is simply to place this company
Export Credits Insurance Act
under the same requirements with respect to income tax and the setting up of reserves as those which apply to insurance companies generally under the legislation that is applicable to them.
And then at page 1724, the hon. member for St. Paul's raised this question. He said:
I understood the parliamentary assistant to say that the corporation was now in a worse position than is a private insurance company. As I read section 2, it seems to me that it would put the corporation in a better position than a private company, in that it may credit to the underwriting reserve any amount it wishes to credit-
The point I wish to make is that what is now proposed is not going to put the Export Credits Insurance Corporation in the same position as the insurance companies, under the section which the parliamentary assistant read, and which provides for the setting up of "such reserves as have been approved for the purpose of this subsection by the superintendent of insurance". That is as different as chalk from cheese from the present proposal, which is that notwithstanding section 12 of the Income Tax Act, the corporation might, in computing its income from its insurance business for a taxation year-
-deduct any amount credited by it pursuant to subsection 2 of this section to the underwriting reserve at the end of such taxation year.
The explanatory note speaks, and, I think, correctly, of "any excess of revenue over expenditure."
The underwriting reserve is defined under subsection 2 of section 11 A as amended by section 5 of chapter 15, Statutes of Canada 1953-54 as follows:
The corporation shall at the end of each fiscal year, if the amount standing to the credit of the underwriting reserve is less than $5 million, credit to the reserve the excess, if any, of its revenues over its disbursements in that fiscal year or so much of the excess as is required to increase the amount of the reserve to $5 million.
I submit with great confidence to the parliamentary assistant that that is as I said as different as chalk from cheese from what we are doing here. Under this provision of the Income Tax Act the insurance company has the right to set up a reserve to the extent approved by the superintendent of insurance. In this bill what is provided is a straight calculation of the amount of receipts and disbursements as the explanatory note says, to find "the excess of revenues over expenditures in each year."
If the situation had been as the parliamentary assistant stated last night, that the effect of this was merely to put the corporation in the position of a privately owned insurance company, I think we would have been in a rather difficult position because we, at the time, were arguing that it should be put in the same position. But I submit,

Export Credits Insurance Act and my colleague from Perth will underline this, that what is now proposed is vastly different; and I submit with some hope to the parliamentary assistant that unless he is able to convince us that we are wrong- and I think he will have some difficulty in doing that-this clause should not be passed today. And, unless we are convinced otherwise, we shall vote against it.
Notwithstanding what I have said, to do what the parliamentary assistant indicated yesterday was his desire, that is, in some way to put this corporation in a position corresponding to that of a privately owned insurance company, seems to me in one way a lot of pother about nothing. The Minister of Finance pointed out in his speech of a few years ago very sensibly, I think:
I do not expect this change to have appreciable net revenue effects. It will increase our tax receipts and reduce our non-tax revenue. All crown company profits eventually find their way into the treasury, and many of them already remit all or the greater part of their profits year by year.
One final point. I am quite unable to understand why, if what the government proposes is carried out, it should really add to the premiums which the Export Credits Insurance Corporation has to charge. As was said yesterday, the corporation has the whole field to itself. After all, this is bookkeeping, and our point is that if the principle laid down by the minister of finance in 1952 was eminently sound-and we believe it was-then the explanation now given is a very substantial departure from it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I appreciate
the concern of the hon. member for Greenwood, and I would sincerely like to have him understand the position as I see it. First of all, toward the end of his remarks he said this corporation has the field to itself. What is the real significance of that, Mr. Chairman? The real significance is that this corporation is by itself in this field for the simple reason that the risks and lack of profit involved are such that no commercial company looking for profits is prepared to go into it. That is the simple reason that it has the field to itself.
This is a corporation that was set up to provide a service for Canadian exporters that no private corporation was prepared to give because they were not in a position to underwrite the possibility of loss and cover that possibility of loss with premiums calculated on an actuarial basis, which is the normal way an insurance company calculates its premiums. For that reason this corporation is not enjoying a monopoly field for some advantage to itself. It is working in a monopoly field because of the inherent

risk involved, and to provide a service that otherwise would not be provided to Canadian exporters.
The position, I submit, is as I stated it yesterday, that the purpose of the amendment is to put the corporation' in the same position as private insurance companies by permitting it to credit to its reserve account the excess of its income in a particular year over its disbursements.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: Is any insurance company allowed to do that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext: I would ask the hon. member to wait a moment. It is permitted to credit the excess of its income over its disbursements to this fund. The private insurance companies are permitted to do the same thing subject to one exception, that being the approval by the superintendent of insurance of the amount they propose to credit to such fund. I am sure the hon. member agrees that that is the position of the private companies. He does not agree that is the position?

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
Not that it is merely a
question of taking in the operating income, but my colleague will deal with that. I will not interrupt.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ADDITIONAL INSURANCE FACILITIES AND RESERVES
speechtext:
In any event, that is the way the section reads, that they are permitted to deduct from their income such amounts paid into policy reserves as have been approved for the purpose of the subsection by the superintendent of insurance. Under the law of this country they are required to get the approval of the superintendent of insurance for the amount they propose to credit to their reserve funds. Once they have that approval the Department of National Revenue then accepts that amount as an allowable deduction for income tax purposes.
This corporation does not come under the jurisdiction of the superintendent of insurance, and in my opening remarks I attempted to indicate very briefly why that is so; that the risks involved in this type of business are such that there is no actuarial basis upon which the superintendent of insurance would be able to fix a proper amount to be put into this corporation's reserve. When the corporation was originally set up it provided for this reserve simply a reserve account. It was found by experience that it would be preferable to have a fixed reserve established in the statute and required to be kept available to meet the possibilities of loss.
Therefore the government took the responsibility, on the advice of its officers, of

recommending to the house that an underwriting reserve up to a maximum of $5 million be set up for the corporation, and that the reserve be provided by crediting to it the entire excess of the corporation's receipts over its disbursements in any year until the reserve totalled $5 million and from that time on any amount that was required to bring it up to the maximum, so that if there was an excess of receipts over disbursements sufficient to bring the fund up to $5 million it would be maintained at that level.
The position of the corporation is that the amount it is entitled to credit to the reserve and the amount of reserve it must maintain are not fixed by the superintendent of insurance but by an act of parliament. The intention of this clause is simply to extend to the corporation the same exemption from the payment of income tax on the amounts paid into the underwriting reserve that applies to private insurance companies on the amounts they are permitted to put into similar reserves under the legislation applying to them, which is the Department of Insurance Act, under which act in their case the approval of the superintendent of insurance is required.
The principle applied to this corporation and the principle applied to private insurance companies are exactly the same. They are both given the privilege of setting up reserves, and in the case of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation their reserve and the method of providing it is fixed by statute. In the case of the private corporations the method of setting up their reserves and the amount they are to credit to a reserve in any year are fixed by the superintendent of insurance, and they have to abide by that.
I submit that the effect of the amendment is exactly as I explained it yesterday, and that the corporation should be permitted to enjoy an exemption from income tax for the purpose of setting up their reserve on exactly the same basis in principle that applies to private corporations; and that is the only purpose of this amendment.

"Proprietary corporations" are those so designated under the Financial Administration Act, and generally speaking are companies which are carrying on business operations similar to and in competition with private business.
It has been made clear by speakers of all parties that no private insurance companies are prepared to enter this field. I am sorry the hon. member for Simcoe North is not in the chamber. speakeroldname: Hon. James Sinclair (Minister of Fisheries) moved
subtopic: SOCKEYE SALMON
subsubtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 180, to implement a convention between Canada and the United States for the protection, preservation and extension of the sockeye salmon fisheries in the Fraser river system, signed at Washington on the 26th day of May, 1930, and a protocol thereto signed at Ottawa on the 28th day of December, 1956.
(Mr. Macdonnell.l
He said: Mr. Speaker, I made very brief remarks at the resolution stage of the bill but said I would spend some time on second reading in describing to the house the very notable success of the international Pacific salmon commission in restoring the great sockeye salmon fishery of the Fraser river. Fisheries scientists around the world agree that this is one of the most remarkable achievements in fisheries management, and I think also that it is an outstanding example of the value of intelligent international cooperation.
The earliest explorers of the north Pacific almost 200 years ago reported the extraordinarily large runs of salmon which they saw moving towards almost every river on the north Pacific coast. Our Indians in British Columbia were known by other Indians as fish eaters because they were almost completely dependent on either dried or smoked salmon as a staple of their diet and, for that matter, they still are heavily dependent on the salmon both as a source of income and as a staple of their diet.
The earliest commercial use made of these salmon was by the trading posts of the Hudson's Bay Company which sent salt and dried salmon down to California at the time of the great gold rush of 1849 and also across to Asia as food for the Asians. The first salmon cannery of British Columbia working on these salmon stocks came into being in the 1860's. These fish were present in such enormous numbers, the actual methods of catching were primitive, so many people thought that this resource was inexhaustible.
Of the five species of Pacific coast salmon the sockeye has always been regarded as the most valuable. It is a 7 pound fish, very red in colour. The red colour maintains itself after cooking. It is very rich in oil and fat. The other species, pink, chum and cohoe salmon, were not used at all before the turn of the century and, in fact, were used very little in the early years of this century. Spring salmon were used a bit at that time. But our entire fishing operation was concentrated on the sockeye salmon and on the sockeye salmon of the Fraser river especially.
As I explained yesterday, because of the route the salmon take coming in from the sea, passing both through American waters and Canadian waters before reaching the mouth of the Fraser river, it was fished by both American fishing fleets and Canadian fishing fleets. In the years 1911, 1912 and 1913, when the C.N.R. was being constructed through the Fraser river canyon, there was considerable damage done to the natural flow of the river, culminating in a very big slide at Hell's Gate in 1913 which so choked the river as to make the flow through the

narrow defile which was left so fast that the great part of the salmon run at high water simply could not fight their way through.
As a consequence of this damage to the river route and as a consequence too of the very high rate of exploitation by both American fishing fleets and Canadian fishing fleets, the salmon runs began to decline, and this naturally alarmed those who were interested in conservation. The late A1 Hager, who was then head of the Canadian Fishing Company, was the one who took the lead in trying to bring about international action to conserve this fishery before it was too late. He had been one of the sponsors of the first international fish treaty in all the world, the Pacific halibut treaty of 1923, which has done so great a job in restoring this high sea fishery for the benefit of both Canadian fishing fleets and American fishing fleets.
In the late 1920's Mr. Hager worked endlessly to have the Americans and Canadians agree to similar conservation for the sockeye salmon of the Fraser system before it was too late. In 1930 the two governments did negotiate such a treaty and the Canadian parliament approved of it as I am asking this house to approve today of this bill. Unfortunately, it was seven long years before congressional and presidential approval of the treaty were secured in the United States. Of course, no action could be taken until both nations had agreed to a joint program.
The reason for this delay was a fairly obvious one. The American fishermen were very reluctant to take part in a new arrangement which was going to divide the sockeye run equally between the two fishing fleets. During those years they were getting about 70 per cent of the fish and our fishermen just 30 per cent. One of the main reasons that they were enjoying so large a part of the catch was that they employed large stationary traps in Puget sound which intercepted the runs as they made their way to the Fraser. It was the sports fishermen in the state of Washington who used their political power and forced the removal of these fish traps. That, and a more aggressive fishing policy by our own fishermen, began to increase the Canadian share of the catch, and finally in 1937 we secured the necessary concurrent approval from the federal government at Washington.
In this seven year period I think the most ardent advocate of such a treaty, next to Mr. Hager himself, was a former member of this house, Tom Reid, who was then the member of parliament for New Westminster, and is now a member of the Senate. New Westminster, of course, is the main town on the Fraser river and was pretty well 82715-111
Fisheries
founded on the salmon industry. He was a persistent champion of this treaty, becoming a member of the salmon commission when it was founded in 1937, and has been a very active member ever since. As a matter of fact, he is the only member of the commission, either Canadian or American, who has served on the commission continuously since its inception in 1937, and I think that without question he is today the great authority on the salmon fishery of the Fraser river.
A number of other notable Canadians have served on the commission. Mr. H. R. MacMillan, for example, who headed our largest fishing company in Canada, is an unusual tycoon in that he is a great scholar as well and he has always shown great interest in the fisheries and was a valued member of the commission. Then there is the chief supervisor of our own department on the west coast, Mr. A. J. Whitmore, whom I regard as one of the ablest officers in the entire public service of Canada.
Once the treaty was approved by the two nations, a period of eight years of study, that is, two full sockeye salmon cycles, was requested before any regulation should be brought into effect. This study was undertaken by the scientific staff of the new commission, and in 1945 they were ready to go ahead with their first works and their first control and regulation. The most important work, of course, was to do something about the slide in the Fraser river canyon at Hell's Gate. It was a very unusual problem in fisheries because nowhere in the fishing world had any fishway been constructed under such circumstances. There are many fish ladders on salmon streams by which salmon can by-pass falls or dams by leaping from pool to pool in an artificial ladder built along the side of the stream, but this was a different problem.
The Fraser, one of the great rivers of the world, rushes through this very narrow canyon and in flood time the level of the river can rise as much as 90 feet in a week. Obviously that would flood out any conventional ladder. The scientists devised an unusual solution, two concrete corridors a little over 100 feet high on either side of the narrow defile in Hell's Gate. These corridors had built in them great vertical baffles coming almost across the corridor to the opposite side so that the water swirling down through these corridors is checked in its speed by the baffles, and little eddies are created behind the baffles in which the fish can rest as they dart up from baffle to baffle, bypassing the fast water in Hell's Gate itself.
These corridors work at any height of water, whether the river is five feet high

Fisheries
or ninety feet high at Hell's Gate. These Hell's Gate fishways were constructed and paid for by the salmon commission under the usual 50-50 sharing agreement between our two governments. The commission has done much more than that though. Hell's Gate is their spectacular achievement, but they have many others. In the entire Fraser river watershed they have built a great number of other smaller fishways to by-pass falls and other natural obstructions. They have opened up spawning beds which were inaccessible to salmon in the natural condition of the river. They have restored fished-out runs. Even in the early days before we had much scientific control of these runs we did have closed periods to allow sufficient salmon through to spawn. But these closed periods did not necessarily tie in with the movements of individual runs of salmon because at that time we had not sufficient scientific knowledge to sort out all the various runs going to the many streams of the Fraser river system, each coming in and going out at a different time. Hence it was quite possible to have the open fishing season last long enough to wipe out an entire run going to some stream. Since then our scientists have done a splendid job in breaking down the sockeye salmon of the entire Fraser system into the various runs, heading for all the different spawning areas. They can identify each run as it enters inland waters and can control the fishing seasons to assure that the peak of each run does get through to the spawning ground. I think that the best evidence of what this commission has done can be given in figures. In the big year cycle, 1954, we had the greatest run of sock-eye salmon since the slide in 1913; and when you consider the rather dismal picture in most other fisheries of the world of a continually diminishing catch, that is a spectacular achievement.
What has been the cost of this commission? We share the cost equally with the federal government of the United States. The Canadian share of the cost of operations-that is payment of staff, maintenance of fishways and things like that-in these 20 years has been $1,576,000. Our share of the construction of the Hell's Gate fishway, the biggest single fishway built, was $1,063,000. The total cost to Canada of operation, maintenance and capital construction was $2,640,000.
Let us now look at the results. I think the fairest way in which to do it is to take the four-year cycle just before the salmon commission moved into the field and then the last four years. The sockeye salmon pack for the years 1933 to 1936 inclusive was 441,126 cases of 48 pounds. There are about

ten 7-pound salmon necessary to make a 48-pound case of canned salmon. In the last four years, 1952 to 1955, inclusive, the pack was 1,203,677 cases. That is the Canadian pack. That is roughly three times as great in volume since the commission started work. The increase in market value, not the total increase since the commission first started operations but just the increase in one four-year cycle, the four-year cycle immediately before the commission started to work and the last four-year cycle-is over $29 million. That is quite an income appreciation on a total investment of just $2,640,000. In addition, the salmon commission are confident that they can increase this catch much more in the years ahead.
The key to the success of the commission, I think, is first of all the very high calibre of the members of the commission. The commission consists of six members, three from each nation, our members being nominated by the government here and the United States members being nominated by the president. We have been fortunate in attracting to this commission outstanding men, both in the scientific field of fisheries and in the industrial field of fisheries. These men serve without remuneration. I think their real reward is the very real achievements which they see they have accomplished. We have gathered together a first-class scientific staff headed by Dr. Loyd Royal, men again who are devoted to this very interesting task of restoring these fisheries over this enormous watershed of the Fraser river.
Another very important factor has been the whole-hearted co-operation of the fishing industry, including both the operators and the fishermen. At first the fishermen I must say were dubious about putting this fishery in the hands of these scientists, "long-haired" scholars who had never actually gone out fishing as commercial fishermen and so of course could not be expected to know as much about fishing as men who had spent their whole life catching fish. It was difficult in the earlier years to convince our fishermen, since we had to cut down on the fishing effort in order to make sure that sufficient fish got through to spawn to rebuild depleted runs. But the years rolled by, and the best evidence of all to the fishermen of the success of the program became manifest through increased catches. Since then we have had the warmest co-operation from the fishermen and the fishing industry. The peak run for sockeye is every four years. In the big run in 1954, at the big peak when millions of salmon were on their way up the Fraser, we had of course a closure in order to ensure that adequate spawning stock, which we like to take off the peak of the run, were getting through, and

so we stopped all fishing. We actually did not need to run a single fisheries patrol vessel on that closed river during that period. Twenty years ago we would have had every patrol vessel and every man we had out there to watch for illegal fishing.
The fishermen's union themselves have been the greatest supporters of the work of this commission, and as a consequence they are all sharing bigger catches.
The very success of this sockeye salmon management has led, of course, to the demand for similar management for the pink salmon on the Fraser river. It is also an international fish in that it follows the same route coming in from the sea through outside Canadian waters on the west coast of Vancouver island, then through the American waters of Puget sound and then back into Canadian waters in the gulf of Georgia before going up the Fraser river. It is just a two-year fish. It goes to sea as soon as it is spawned. It is a smaller fish. It averages about five pounds. Before world war I this fish was scarcely used at all in Canada. Our canneries did not accept it. There was some small sale for it locally. Our Canadian people, and especially our British customers, preferred the rich, red sockeye salmon. They thought that the paler pink salmon was not as good a fish, although the food value of the two is almost identical. The Americans used to get 90 per cent of those runs and our fishermen 10 per cent. In good years those runs used to amount to 30 million fish. Since world war I the Canadian catch has slowly increased. After world war II it amounted to about 20 per cent. But there was a great increase in market demand for this fish, and the market for it rose. The fish which used to bring only five cents for a whole fish, last season brought an average price of about nine cents a pound, or 45 cents per fish. However, our fishermen were alarmed because the pink runs seemed to be declining again because of very heavy fishing effort, mainly on the American side. The government of Canada realized that our fishermen have been most anxious for such a pink salmon conservation treaty for some time.
When speaking a couple of days ago on this matter, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich had this to say, as reported at page 1688 of Hansard:
It would seem, however, that for some reason or other the government has been unwilling to take the initiative in introducing such legislation until very recent times.
We have not been unwilling. Unfortunately, it takes two to make such an agreement. He went on to say this:
Of course the United States government was not the least bit interested.
82715-111J
Fisheries
I think that is not quite fair to the United States government. They have shown interest. It was the United States fishermen who were not the least bit interested for the very simple reason that they were getting 80 per cent of the catch and they could not see much point in an international treaty which would limit them to just 50 per cent of the catch. There was no question, however, that our Canadian fishermen wanted such a treaty.
Not long after I became minister almost five years ago, I attended the annual convention of the fishermen's union in British Columbia and this was one of the questions immediately put to me. What did I intend to do about the pink salmon? I said I intended to do my best to see that a treaty was arrived at, but the question was how? Since the only obstacle seemed to be the fact that the United States fishermen were not enthused because they were getting 80 per cent of the fish and our men 20 per cent of the fish, there was only one way to attack the problem and that was to outfish the United States fishermen. The program which I announced to the union the following year was designed to do that. We could outfish the United States fishermen because of our geographical position. The fish come from the high seas and enter Canadian waters on the outside of Vancouver island before passing through United States waters and then into Canadian waters again in the gulf of Georgia where our fleet normally caught them.
We did not have the boats and gear with which to fish out on the open Pacific Canadian waters and I encouraged our fishing companies and fishermen to purchase 15 big old deep-sea seiners which were available in the United States at a very low cost. I had to persuade my colleague the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) to waive the Canada Steamship Regulations which forbid the importation of ships more than five years old. As an incentive my colleague the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) agreed to remit half of the duty on those ships after the first year's fishing in outside waters and the other half of the duty after the second year's fishing. I, for my part, told the fishermen that all restrictions on the size of the gear they chose to use were off when they fished these outside waters, and the usual weekly closure on Saturday and Sunday would also be removed. I told them to go out there and fish and get our share before the fish entered American waters. I can assure you I kept the United States interests informed of this policy, and assured them also that though we were starting a fishing war we would much rather have a conservation treaty. If we could not have a treaty,

Fisheries
we would try to get a lion's share of what was left of the fishery.
Well, it worked out very well. The big run of pinks came in two years ago and our catch rose to 46 per cent. Instead of the usual 80-20, the United States got 54 per cent and we got 46 per cent. We would have obtained a higher percentage than the United States fishermen except for one little thing. On the west coast our fishermen have long been on the five-day week, long before the five-day week was effective in industrial employment. On the Fraser and these other salmon streams we have always automatically closed on Saturday and Sunday to allow at least two-sevenths of the salmon to pass up to the spawning grounds. And recently we have had to have even longer closures. The fishermen who went outside to catch these pinks by force of habit came in on Saturday and Sunday even though we had opened this area to continuous fishing. Thus for two days a week the American fleet in Puget sound got first crack at the incoming salmon schools.
When I spoke to the fishermen's convention the next spring I reproved them for coming in and giving the Americans two days clear fishing. If I had been home-I was in hospital in Russia at the time-I would have urged them during the fishing season. I told them that next season they were to go out and fish seven days a week. They answered that it was very easy for me to request that because I did not go out on the open Pacific in storms and fog, seven days a week living in cramped quarters handling heavy fishing gear. They said they had to have time off, so I suggested that they arrange a rotation of days off, not necessarily Saturday and Sunday, so that we would always have a Canadian fleet out seven days a week. The union was not very enthused about this at first because they could not see any lasting advantage in a fishing war. However, they became enthused later and I was sure that this coming year with this program we would get the major share of the pink salmon.
At the same time, however, our government made formal representations to the United States government that we would like to engage in a pink salmon treaty under the sockeye salmon protocol. We got a helpful reply from the United States government, and that government then got a good reaction from the fishermen of Washington anfi Oregon. The United States delegation came here last fall and in four days we negotiated this treaty which was then signed in December. The treaty put the pink salmon under the control and administration of the international Pacific salmon commission

which, up to now, has just controlled the sockeye salmon of the Fraser system. The commission will start with a six year study program on the pink salmon and other Fraser species as well, the cohoe, springs and chums. Unlike the first years of the sockeye salmon commission work we are not going to wait six years before we regulate the pink salmon fisheries. Regulation will start immediately and the sharing of the catch will start immediately.
The present salmon commission is, without question, the best body to carry out this work. There was some talk that we should set up a separate commission on pink salmon, but that would be unfortunate because the area of administration for sockeye and pinks is identical. Certainly our fishermen today have great confidence in the staff of the international Pacific salmon commission because of their achievements. A great deal of the work already done for the sockeye salmon has proven very beneficial for the pink salmon. From 1913 on after the slide in Hell's Gate there had been no pink salmon on the Fraser above Hell's Gate. These small salmon simply could not forge their way through the increased speed of the flow of the Fraser river. Soon after the construction of the Hell's Gate fishway the Department of Fisheries noticed pink salmon spawning on the Fraser as far as Lytton and up on the Thompson river. Therefore, some of the work which has been done for the sockeye salmon has improved the pink salmon as well.
So much for the pink salmon: since the act is opened for the first time in 20 years, you will notice that there are one or two other amendments which the commission wanted in view of the experience they have garnered in these 20 years. We are putting this in the same form as other international fisheries treaties signed since that time. Last year, you may remember, I had a difference, the only difference we have ever had with the salmon commission, because I refused to enforce one of their regulations. In the old protocol there was a stipulation that if the salmon commission closed fishing in any part of Canadian waters it had to be closed in all Canadian waters. If fishing were closed in any part of the United States waters, it had to be closed in all United States waters. Last year the salmon commission requested that we close fishing in the outside Canadian waters and maintain it in the inside Canadian waters. This was quite contrary to the protocol which parliament had approved, and I said we could not enforce it. I suggested to them that if

they wanted this change they should put it forward and we would amend the act, as we are now doing.
The commission themselves do not do the enforcing of the regulations. The two governments do that. The state of Washington acts for the federal government since in the United States the states have control over fishing, and our Department of Fisheries acts in our country. These arrangements have worked out very well, but in recent years we have had the feeling that regulations for enforcement should not be left solely to an international commission. The new convention provides that these regulations must be approved by the governments concerned. I think most of the people in parliament will agree that too much authority in law enforcement should not be handed over to even as good a commission as this.
There is just one other thing I should like to mention. A couple of days ago the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) spoke to me, and in his speech the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) mentioned that all the good work which this commission has done in restoring this extremely valuable British Columbia resource, and all the good work we hope they are going to do in rebuilding the pink salmon fishery, will go out the window if the power interests of British Columbia are permitted to dam the Fraser river. In reply to the observations made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra yesterday at the resolution stage, I outlined the position of the Department of Fisheries and the fishing industry of British Columbia on this matter. It does not matter whether you call the problem fish versus power or fish and power, however you describe it, but we like to think of it as fish and power.
One of the difficulties encountered is the failure of the ordinary layman to understand the very great problems facing the fishing industry in this matter. Not long ago I spoke to the mining institute of western Canada and I was asked to speak on this very subject because power is essential to mining. The miners could not understand why it was so difficult to move an adult salmon up over a dam and then 20 times as many small salmon down over a dam, since much greater transportation problems were quickly solved in their industry. They pointed out that in their industry they move millions of tons of rock and ore from the bowels of the earth to the surface. Moving big things upward relates to moving adult salmon over dams. Moving small things down in the mining industry-the rock and ore which goes through the crushers and on to the screens of the mill, movement of large amounts of
Fisheries
things much more minute than the finger-lings we want to move down over the dams. That seemed to me to be an extremely reasonable observation from a mining point of view.
Today I am going to attempt just briefly to describe to you in layman's language why it is these very brilliant scientists of the fishery nations of the world and our engineers have not as yet been able to solve our transportation problems as easily as the miners have solved their problem.
I think it would be easiest if we were to take the sockeye salmon cycle and discuss its life history because it is the fish most valuable in the Fraser system and which presents the greatest problem. The sockeye salmon has an extraordinary homing instinct. I think it is unequalled by any other animal in the world. Towards the end of the fourth year of its life the adult salmon is out in the north Pacific. Some primeval urge in the early summer turns it toward the strait of Juan de Fuca. It heads for the south end of Vancouver island, around the south end of the island through the waters of Puget sound into the gulf of Georgia where it mills around for two or three days in the estuary of the Fraser river before starting up the Fraser river seeking out in that enormous watershed the little creek in which it was spawned four years before.
As I have said the homing instinct of the sockeye salmon is quite fantastic. Our scientists have found out by tagging that over 95 per cent of the sockeye return to the little creek in which they were spawned despite the fact that the creek may be located 800 miles up the Fraser river.
These salmon stop feeding once they come near fresh water and throughout the course of their long journey up the river to spawn they live on the food and energy stored in their own bodies. The sockeye salmon goes the farthest of all salmon and that is why it is so rich and in such a fat condition. Having sought out-we think mainly by taste *-the little creek in which they were spawned, the male and female spawn and die. In the springtime the little salmon fry emerge from the egg and drift down to the lake below, where they usually spend one year or sometimes two years and in those lakes they grow to the smolt stage. They then pass down the river and reverse the trip travelling around Puget sound, the south end of Vancouver island and out to sea for a three year sojourn.
Well, now, let us consider the effect on this migration of a power dam on the Fraser river. We will consider just one dam on the Fraser river and the effect it would have on this age old cycle of movement of salmon-

Fisheries
are concerned the cost of power from gas must be getting close to the cost of obtaining power from hydro.
Finally, I would say that we are just on the verge of the atomic age as far as the production of electric power for commercial use is concerned. Britain has two commercial plants in operation already. Every British Columbian should remember, too, that the cost of hydro power from a salmon stream is not the same as the cost of hydro power on a non-salmon stream, because the cost of hydro power on a salmon stream must include both the cost of the dam and the necessary installations plus the cost of the fishways which under the Fisheries Act we can oblige the company to build. In the case of the Fraser river, the dams which the B. C. Electric is planning, these fishways would cost, according to our estimate, somewhere around $300 million-not very effective fishways, either.

speechtext:
am sure the house is indebted to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) for his very comprehensive review of the background which led up to the introduction of this bill. He gave us considerable historical data regarding the establishment of the International Pacific Salmon Commission which was originally set up in 1930. Then he dealt with the life history of our various species of salmon and then with the work of the commission which I am sure justifies the request that the commission now look after the pink salmon as well as the sockeye. Then he gave us a very full and detailed account of the effect of power developments on the salmon run. All of what was most interesting and is valuable information to have on the record. I hope he will not consider it as carping criticism if I say that perhaps he might have spent a little more time explaining the actual bill itself and the protocol attached to the bill. No doubt when he is summing up at the conclusion of the debate he will be able to give us more information on that point.
As I said when speaking at the resolution stage, we believe that the objects of the bill,

which is intended to implement the convention between Canada and the United States for the protection and preservation of the sockeye salmon and, by extending the provisions of that convention, to cover also the pink salmon, are wholly commendable. It is essential, as I said yesterday, that this great national resource be preserved. A continuation of the fishing war which the minister described this afternoon might have exterminated not only the sockeye but also the pink salmon because, as the minister knows, the runs of the sockeye, the pink and the other species do overlap to a certain extent and in some cases take place simultaneously.
If fishermen are allowed to use indiscriminately in narrow waters the modern equipment which can catch literally tons and tons of fish in a very short time and are allowed to use in narrow waters the type of nets which are used in the ocean, our fish would certainly be exterminated in the not too distant future. It is obvious that if this desirable end, the conservation of our fish, is to be achieved it can only be done by the combined efforts of Canada and the United States, and the bill is intended to bring about that end. The governments of the United States and Canada have intimated that they would like to use the international Pacific fisheries commission as the medium for achieving that end, and from what the minister has told us this afternoon of the excellent work done by that commission I feel he has fully justified the decision to extend the scope of that commission so that it can deal not only with the sockeye but also with the pink salmon.
The minister has explained the value of the pink runs, and I referred to that yesterday afternoon. The total value of the catch amounts to tens of thousands of dollars and it is a very valuable contribution to the economy of the country and the many thousands of fishermen employed in the industry. Therefore we cannot overemphasize the importance of taking these measures.
To come to the actual bill itself and the protocol, the minister referred to one important amendment which is being introduced, a deletion which may have very far-reaching repercussions because, as he said, in article IV of the convention of 1930 the commission is empowered to exercise certain limiting and prohibiting powers with respect to the taking of sockeye in certain territorial waters and in the high seas. That article of the original treaty goes on to refer to the catching of these fish both in Canadian and American waters which have been

previously described in the first article, namely, the Canadians waters of the Fraser river and the waters immediately adjacent to the mouth of the Fraser river and certain American waters.
The article states, as the minister mentioned this afternoon, that when prohibition is applied it must apply to all the waters in question, all the territorial waters, all the Canadian waters or all the American waters. The minister referred to the difficulties which arose a year ago. After a good deal of discussion, I believe, the commission decided to prohibit first of all the catching of sockeye salmon in Canadian waters during a certain period of last year.

speechtext:
Outside, yes. May I say in the Canadian portion of the international waters. That resulted in very considerable objections from the Canadian fishermen and I asked some questions in the house last year about the matter. As the result of the objection raised by our own department, I believe, and certainly by the minister and by some of the Canadian members on the commission, that limited prohibition was extended so as to cover all waters, both on the American side and on the Canadian side. I think I should quote the remarks made by the minister when speaking on March 2, 1956. They will be found at page 1747 of Hansard. I must quote at length because I feel this is a very important amendment which is being suggested. At that time the minister said:
One of the proposals made by the salmon commission, and one which was mentioned in a question earlier this session by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, was the proposal that all fishing be stopped in outside Canadian waters. It is only in recent years that we have actually begun to fish those waters. Before the sockeye would swing around the end of Vancouver island into the strait of Juan de Fuca, where the United States fishermen would get their half of the fish. The sockeye would then go into the gulf of Georgia and up the Fraser river where our fishermen would get their half of the fish. In recent years, especially since the last war, we have encouraged the fishermen to get out to sea and establish historic rights on the high sea fishery, and also to put us in a little better position. In the past, we got the second half of the fish.
The minister confirmed those statements this afternoon. Then later on he went on to say this:
This proposal, X am informed by my legal advisers, is in direct contravention of the commission treaty which was approved by this house in 1937. Article 4 of the treaty says that if any of the Canadian waters are to be closed, all the Canadian waters are to be closed; if any of the United States waters are to be closed, all the United States waters are to be closed. It is quite true that over the years there may have been minor variations in that we did agree upon closing inside areas for week end closures of different lengths, but never have we agreed, in violation of the treaty, to a complete
Fisheries
closure of a very important Canadian fishing area. I have, therefore, written the chairman of the international commission telling him, first of all, that this is in contravention of the treaty approved by this parliament, and while 1 have the power as Minister of Fisheries under the Fisheries Act to order such a closure, I was not given the power by this parliament to exercise it under the terms of the international Pacific salmon convention. I have asked him, therefore, to reconsider the proposal and see whether the same conservation results can be achieved without this precedent of completely closing an important Canadian area, an area which is of very great importance to us in other fisheries as well as in the sockeye salmon fishery at the moment.
It seems to me that the action then taken by the minister was highly commendable. It met with the wishes of my constituents who were vitally concerned as well as the fishermen who came from the mainland and fished off the southern end of Vancouver island. It seems to me that it was wise that the Canadian government should retain that power and deny the commission the right to close certain areas while leaving other areas open. The feeling last year was that the Canadian fishermen were being discriminated against by the ruling of this commission and that the United States fishermen would once again have all the advantages which they enjoyed before the commencement of a fishing war which the minister described this afternoon when the introduction of bigger vessels and better equipment enabled our Canadian fishermen to hold their own with the United States fishermen. I cannot help feeling that we are turning the clock back and that we are surrendering the power which the government had, by saying to the commission that they have full authority to close any part of the conservation area, whether it be on the Canadian side or on the United States side; that they are not obliged to close the whole of the waters concerned; and that we are leaving the matter entirely to the discretion of this international commission.
We have great admiration for the work which the commission has done. That commission is composed half of Americans and half of Canadians or, in other words, three Canadians and three Americans. It does seem to me to be unwise that we should surrender the right of the Canadian government to allow this international commission to close off perhaps part of our waters and not put the same restrictions upon the United States waters. Surely we should insist on a general policy. I mention a general policy because, as the minister said last year, there have been minor changes which are desirable. But at the commencement of the fishing season surely we should insist upon the policy of equal treatment in all areas. That is not written into the protocol. I suppose

Fisheries
nothing could be written in there. But I should like to have from the minister a definite statement which will show that the rights of the Canadian fishermen can be protected by the Canadian government and that we are not handing all of those rights over entirely to this international commission.
I wish to continue quoting from page 1748 of Hansard of last year. When the minister was speaking last year, afte rmaking the remarks which I have just quoted, he went on to say this:
I told the chairman that the Canadian people are most appreciative of the magnificent job the commission has done in re-establishing this great fishery. I said that if, over the years the commission has found from its experience that certain articles of the convention are hampering its work, then we in this parliament certainly would be very glad to hear its recommendation for change, and that would be the proper way to do it.
I presume that the commission has made certain representations to the government saying that its work has been hampered because of the clause which enunciated the policy of equal treatment in all areas. I hope the minister will be able to give us examples, either when he is replying or at some other time, although I think it should be done here while we are considering second reading because, in my opinion, this is an extremely important amendment. If he would tell us how the commission feel their work has been hampered because of this restriction which I described as enunciating the policy of equal treatment in all areas, we would be grateful.
It may be that the amendment which is suggested to article 6 may be a qualifying clause. I do not know whether it applies to the exact point that I have raised because there it stipulates that the regulations of the commission are subject to the approval of the two governments. That would seem to be wise because we must have the authority. It also deals with the opening fishing periods in the various areas. I am not quite certain whether that refers to the so-called outside waters or whether it refers only to the strictly Canadian or United States waters. However, I want to have the minister's assurance that in that qualifying clause there is ample protection-for the Canadian fishermen and that it will prevent the possibility of this commission's closing off certain areas and leaving other areas open.
Now, that is the main point to which I wanted to refer. I believe there are other points which will have to be discussed when this bill goes to the marine and fisheries committee to which I understand the minister intends to send it. There is just one point which is akin to this policy of equal treatment in all areas, and that really concerns

the equal treatment given to the different kinds of fishing gear. I know that is a very debatable subject both on the west coast amongst fishermen themselves and with the government. If we are having the commission or the department exercise the right to close off certain areas for certain periods, as must be done, then consideration must be given to a fair division of the catch, not only between United States and Canadian fishermen but between the gill net fishermen and the seiners. I believe I am correct in saying that the association of fish boat owners and also the union feel that some steps should be taken to ensure that both the gill net fleet and the seiners have a fair share of the catch.
I understand that some sort of mutual agreement has been worked out on the gulf of Georgia whereby the gill netters fish during the hours of darkness and the seiners commence their operations after daybreak. No such gentlemen's agreement, may I call it, exists in so far as the two fleets are concerned as they get farther out to sea. Certainly, I do not think there is any such agreement as between United States and Canadian fishermen on the basis of the two different types of equipment used. The government has the power to close the various areas. The government has the power to restrict fishing in areas which would be mainly fished by the seiners or mainly fished by the gill netters.
The advantages of the gill net or the seine seem to change from time to time. At one period all the advantages were with the gill netters, and then the pendulum swung and the advantage went to the seiners. It may well be now that the advantage is swinging back to the gill netters owing to the new types of equipment they have. I understand these nylon nets are giving the gill netter quite an advantage. I believe I am correct in saying that there were regulations enforced in 1954 which to a certain extent assured a division between the two. I believe the minister speaking in Vancouver that year indicated he thought some division should be made. There seems to have been a change in that policy in recent years.

Mr. Speaker, like others who have taken part in this debate, I welcome this particular measure and congratulate the minister on having succeeded finally in getting this convention signed. I may say I was very much struck with his description of what I suppose one could call his pragmatic diplomacy by which he achieved the purposes of his department, and when he was telling us about it I wondered if it was not perhaps an example for our whole Department of External Affairs in dealing with intractable neighbours on all sides. However, it was, as I say, a very sensible piece of diplomacy that enabled us to have this convention signed.
I think also it is significant in another way in that it is a further example of the way in which free nations can co-operate for some specific purpose the value of which is perfectly obvious to all of them. It may
Fisheries
indeed be the foundation for a more wide-reaching and fundamental co-operation in the future.
I was also very relieved to hear the minister tell us his department is determined that there shall be no destruction of the salmon runs on the Fraser river in British Columbia because we have had some very disturbing reports from our province of British Columbia. There have been suggestions that the powers that be in that province are going to make what I think would be an extremely short-sighted choice, the choice between having more aluminum and having salmon. I realize of course that it is coming perilously close to blasphemy to suggest that perhaps the salmon in the streams of British Columbia are of more ultimate value to the human race than more aluminum to build planes that will be obsolete before they come off the assembly line or for any of the other uses to which the power that is being sought might be put. I believe that we have to combat this-I can only describe it as a cheap scale of values that are abroad in the world today.
I have been reading some of the statements made by various people in British Columbia on this question. There are two statements made by two people in which I find an extremely interesting contrast. The author of one of these statements is a professor in British Columbia. I believe his field is geology but he has not hesitated to inform the world at large that it is possible to make the best of both worlds and to have power and salmon. He does not mention any biological eminences who support him but at any rate throughout all his prophecies there steals the viewpoint that it is more important that we should have power for undetermined reasons to produce goods of varying values and that if necessary we should destroy the salmon in the British Columbia streams for that purpose. Set against his comments are the numerous public utterances of an eminent naturalist, a constituent of my friend the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), Mr. Robert Haig Brown.

Last fall I had the pleasure of listening to Mr. Haig Brown speak on this very question of the preservation of the salmon runs of British Columbia, and even more fundamentally the preservation of at least some part of the natural background of life on this continent.
Mr. Haig Brown stressed the immensely important psychological values of not destroying all the natural background that we inherited on this continent and I believe that is a matter we are going to have to consider

Fisheries
more and more as time goes on. We are going to have to realize that there are other measurements than production of material goods and there are measurements other than dollars; there are measurements in human satisfactions.
I recall my own boyhood in British Columbia when I lived alongside a small stream that flows into Burrard inlet, which is now of course the harbour of the metropolis of Vancouver, and I remember that every year we used to watch the salmon come swarming up that stream, the miracle of the returning salmon. Of course they do not come now to any extent because it has been destroyed by the process of industrialization, but I think it would be a tragedy if future generations of British Columbians were to be deprived of seeing that astonishing and inspiring natural miracle. You cannot put its value in dollars or cents nor can you measure it by material standards but it has a very real and important value in our society.
I think we are going to have to learn to fit ourselves as human beings into what biologists call our ecology. We have had the curious idea that it is our role as a species to dominate and control all other species and to dominate all natural forces. I suggest that the time is coming when we are going to have to realize that we have to co-operate with all other natural forces if we are going to survive as a species and if we are going to be able to build anything in the way of a worth-while human society.
Some while ago a friend of mine handed me a book that is very appropriate to the discussion we have had today. It is a book by Professor Ashley Montagu whom some of you may recall as the rash man who publicly said what all of the rest of us have the sense to keep quiet about, that women are the superior sex.

Professor Montagu's book is entitled, "Darwin-Competition and Co-Operation". In it he takes issue with the old Darwinian idea of "nature red in tooth and craw" and "the survival of the fittest" and so forth, and he has this to say part way through his book:
" 'Don't compete!-competition is always injurious to the species, and you have plenty of resources to avoid it!' That is the tendency of nature, not always realized in full, but always present. That is the watchword which comes to us from the bush, the forest, the river, the ocean. 'Therefore combine -practice mutual aid! That is the surest means for giving to each and to all the greatest safety, the best guarantee of existence and progress, bodily, intellectual, and moral.' That is what nature teaches us."
[Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo) .J
I think that when we face a choice such as we seem to have with regard to hydroelectric power and the salmon runs of the British Columbian rivers then this is the point of view we shall have to take into consideration, the fact that man is a part of his environment and he must co-operate with his environment.
If he destroys it, he destroys himself. The minister stated this afternoon, or on Friday, that once destroyed these things can never be brought back again. We can knock down the dams when we find they are useless, we can destroy the factories we have built when we find that we are not particularly interested in the things the factories are making, but the salmon will not come back. The life that was there will be gone for good and when it goes the lives of all those human beings who live in that area will be just that much poorer.
So I trust the minister will continue to oppose any shortsighted moves for immediate gain which will destroy one of the most distinctive features, perhaps the most distinctive, of the natural history of our province, that is the salmon runs on our rivers, and that he will seek to find co-operation, not only among other nations but among our own citizens for the preservation of what is to my mind an absolutely priceless asset.

Mr. Speaker, it is my intention tonight to deal with one or two aspects of this matter which I either failed to complete yesterday or had just touched upon. Before I do so may I say that I am reminded of what the minister said early in his remarks this afternoon when he paid such a fine compliment to the sockeye salmon commission and the work it has done in past years. I agree completely with the minister that possibly the restoration of the sockeye salmon run that we find today is due largely to the ardent work that Senator Reid has done in the past. If I did not misinterpret his words, the minister indicated this afternoon that the United States fishermen had been pretty well brought to their senses during the season of 1955 when the division of catch was 54-46 I believe. I am fully aware that the suggestion about that had been made two years previously, but it was not a matter of waiting until 1955. I find among my notes the following:
Joe Burrows, president of the Puget sound gill-netters' association said his organization had not made any decision as yet but his own personal feeling was in favour of joint control of the fishery. He promised to go back and report the findings of this conference to his membership and he was quite sure his membership would take a favourable stand. He wondered if pinks should be put under international control how this would affect or how it might interrupt the inner Puget sound fishery.
He was concerned that it might hurt the small boat fishermen. Apparently in the United States they have the same problem in connection with gillnetters that we have. The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) referred to this problem facing our own gillnet fishermen.
Dick Kink of the Puget sound vessel owners said that as far as conservation was concerned his personal opinion was that there was no question but that this must be supported to the fullest.
