This is agreed to also by the I.L.W.U. and the united fishermen's allied workmen's union. The actual fact is that there has been a growing feeling about this among fishermen on the Pacific coast, Americans as well as Canadians, who have come to realize the true worth of the sockeye salmon commission, of which we have spoken so highly, that they endorse the plan completely.
In so far as fishing on the high seas is concerned, I have only a brief comment to make as I referred to this yesterday. I have
Fisheries
reread what the minister had to say and I think his explanation is a good one. I would urge that we begin now to attempt to establish a limit on the distance offshore that fishing can be done, not just between ourselves and the United States but on an international basis, as has I understand been the case in Iceland to a degree.
The minister agreed yesterday that salmon fisheries on the high seas were made up mostly of smaller fish. Apparently it takes about twice as many fish to complete the same size pack as it would take along the coastline. The preservation of salmon, or any fish for that matter other than deep sea fish, I submit should be encouraged and fishing should be confined to the coastal area. Now that we have reached this point of accomplishment I urge the minister to begin working on an international agreement or convention to limit fishing on the high seas to only fish which might be termed high seas fish, and to provide that those fish that reach complete maturity along the coastline should be permitted to be caught only in those areas.
Yesterday I read a letter from an Alberta resident which was of particular interest to the committee and to the minister, and his remarks were certainly timely. The reason for observations in that letter was brought out definitely by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron), who has just referred to the false idea of thinking that we can build dams and at the same time have fish. There has been so much loose talk about the ability to carry on power projects on our salmon fishing rivers, such as the Fraser, and at the same time preserve the salmon, that I felt and still feel that it is necessary that the scientists who are connected with the fishing industry, the minister himself and all those in authority should indicate just how they feel about the matter, because the point has not yet been reached where we can carry on power projects and preserve our fishing industry at the same time.
This is particularly true, as the minister himself pointed out with respect to the sockeye salmon industry. I was particularly interested in the viewpoint of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) which reminded me of the debate last year in which the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) raised the same question. As I recall it, this year the minister reiterated once again that as far as he and his department were concerned they would not permit any development of power dams along the Fraser river until such time as the fishing industry would not be in jeopardy.

Fisheries
Last year, as recorded at page 1975 of Hansard, for March 9, I find the minister represented by a quotation to which the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam referred, He said:
We feel, first of all, that every non-salmon stream in the province should be developed for power before a salmon stream is touched. In that respect we feel that before the Fraser is touched that part of the Columbia river in Canada should be exploited to the full.
And the minister is still in agreement with his utterance of last year. I am satisfied that every hon. member from British Columbia probably feels in exactly the same way. I do, and the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) has indicated the same thing.
On the same page of Hansard, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam says:
I hope the minister is very keenly aware of the fact that unless the federal government, which last year assumed some responsibility for power development on the Columbia river, undertakes some initiative in the matter of early development of power in the Columbia basin, the federal government may find the provincial government making a deal that will completely frustrate the good intentions of the minister. Because of the failure of initiative on the part of the federal government, we may see the British Columbia government take some action that most Canadians might have reason to regret.
That statement was made shortly after the minister had spoken. I did not have time to re-examine the whole of the minister's remarks in the course of that debate, but I can distinctly remember him saying that the British Columbia government had given an assurance that it was not going to permit any damming of the Fraser river at this time, and it is for that reason that I rise in my place now to draw that fact to the attention of the house. Neither the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam nor any other hon. member should take it upon himself to decide what the government of any province is, possibly, going to do, particularly in the light of what the minister himself said. I view that with a great deal of alarm.
We must remember that the debate I spoke of took place on March 9, 1956. I have in my hand a statement of policy from the Vancouver board of trade dated December 15, 1955, respecting fishery and power resources in British Columbia. In this brief, issued some months before the statement to which I have referred was made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, I find the board has this to say on page 2 of the document:
The industry contends that the fishery should be preserved and expanded through the application of scientific knowledge.
The board of trade's members, as industrialists, realize the value of the fishing industry

to our province. I am sure there is not a single citizen in my province who does not realize the extent of its value, and while there are interests which would like to dam the Fraser river, they realize that in doing so they would deprive us of one of our inheritances and one of the industries which have been with us since the birth of British Columbia, and long before that time, as the minister has pointed out.
The board of trade went on to say:
They (industry) recognize the need for continual increase of power development in this province but have advocated that power requirements he developed where it is available on "non-fish producing" rivers and from other energy sources.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that it is necessary to put this matter on record if for no other reason than to let the people of Canada know that despite the tremendous growth of industry in my own province today industry still recognizes that we must not dam the Fraser river until such time as we can be assured that the salmon industry will survive.
The statement of policy continues, and has this to say about the provincial government:
The provincial government has also recognized these principles and incorporated them in an amendment to the provincial fisheries act at the last session of the provincial legislature.
Thus, early in 1955, one year before the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam spoke and cast the reflection he did, the government of the province had recognized what the minister recognizes now and had recognized at that time. He recognized it during the debate on Bill No. 3, if I recall it correctly, when we were discussing Canadian rivers.
At this time may I appeal to the minister to use his persuasive powers, since he apparently has them with this government and with certain associates in the United States as well, to see whether we cannot expedite the development which we hope to see on the Columbia river so that we may at least come to some formal agreement with the Americans with regard to responsibility and the delegation thereof. As was indicated by the board of trade, we are very much in need of power. We realize that only too well. However, I wish to draw this to the attention of the house because I do not think it is fair to the people of my province or to the interests within my province to have the impression left abroad which was given a year ago by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, namely that certain interests in British Columbia were so power-hungry that they were going to deprive us of our salmon industry.
The minister, who is very alert with regard to the matters in which hon. members from British Columbia are interested, has

been good enough to send me a pamphlet entitled "Downstream Fish Migration Over Dams". Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of holding up the debate unduly but there are two points I want to raise. In the first place, I have a specific question for the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) which I hope he will answer either when he winds up this stage of the debate or when we are in committee on the bill. While the whole of the country and certainly the whole of British Columbia are delighted with the successful outcome of the negotiations which have resulted in the agreement respecting the inshore fishermen, will the minister let us know exactly what is the state of affairs with regard to the offshore fishing as between the two countries?
I think that I would be remiss in my duty as a private member of parliament from British Columbia if I did not add my little token of praise of this really great achievement. When we sit here year after year and have so many contentious debates and when we know that a rather hot election is just in the offing, it is certainly a gratifying experience to hear members of all parties get up one after the other and compliment the Minister of Fisheries. I think this is one of the greatest diplomatic achievements on record with respect to the relations between our two countries.
When I thought of what the Minister of Fisheries had actually achieved, for some reason or other I thought of the great seal of the United States on which the American eagle is shown with an olive branch in one hand and a cluster of arrows in the other. I certainly think our Minister of Fisheries is a most ambidextrous person because while I would not say that in the negotiations with the United States he had a two-fisted approach he did have a two-handed approach. He held out one hand offering friendship on a fair and sane basis and while I will not say that he held out a threat with the other hand he certainly held out a challenge to the United States that unless they were willing to make an aboveboard agreement fair to both countries which would conserve this great natural resource we would be forced to take other measures.
It seems to me that one of the greatest tributes that could be paid to the Minister of Fisheries is this. There are some things that a cabinet minister can do by reason of the fact that he is a cabinet minister and can initiate legislation in the house which becomes the law of the country. But it seems to me it is a far greater tribute to any leader in political life when his moral force is

such that he can appeal directly to the citizenry of the country and get them to follow him with respect to a proposal that he regards as good.
If ever there was a case when we had an enlightened leader of the people of Canada giving intelligent leadership to a certain group in Canada, we had that evidence when the Minister of Fisheries appealed directly to the fishermen of British Columbia and told them to go out and out-fish our good cousins, the Americans, with what happy result we all know. Because I think the Minister of Fisheries has had such great and conspicuous success with regard to the future of this great natural resource which is so important to us in British Columbia, I look forward to even greater things in the future along the same line.

I also want to make it quite clear that I do not want to see any development of a discussion of what I would call the internal politics of British Columbians in this debate. But in view of the references he made to a speech which was previously made in this house by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) I think that perhaps I should point out that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and some of the rest of us in British Columbia had some considerable concern a time ago about some reported statements which were attributed to a leading minister in the Social Credit cabinet in the province of British Columbia. I am referring to press reports of statements made by Mr. Gaglardi, the minister of highways, which led many of us to believe that the British Columbia government might be prepared to take a position and acquiesce in the sacrifice of our Fraser river salmon resources to the development of power at the Moran dam site. I recognize that to the best of my knowledge the government of British Columbia has clearly taken a position now that, as far as their legislative action is concerned, they will require that proper review and consent be given by the Department of Fisheries before the water rights branch will grant licences. I for one am very glad that they have taken

that position and I hope that they will continue to hold it. But I think that the record should be clear at this point that there was one particular stage when some of us had, in my opinion, real cause for concern in view of reported statements, as I say, by a leading member of the British Columbia cabinet. While I have not those references here with me in the house now, I am quite sure that it was those statements which the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam had in mind when he spoke at the time to which the hon. member for New Westminster refers.
I am not going to continue the discussion further at this stage of the debate, Mr. Speaker. I had an opportunity of saying something at the resolution stage. I think my colleague, the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron), has indicated clearly that we are in full support of the principle of the bill that is now before us. We are looking forward to the meetings that will be held of the marine and fisheries committee on the details of the legislation.

subtopic: SOCKEYE SALMON
subsubtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we had the opportunity this afternoon of listening to an extremely interesting resume of events and negotiations leading up to the signing of the protocol bringing the pink salmon under the terms of the convention existing between Canada and the United States for the preservation and expansion of the sockeye salmon fisheries in the Fraser river system. I agree with the other hon. members who have taken part in this debate that this is a desirable objective that has been achieved and it, of course, will receive the full and enthusiastic support of all the fishermen of British Columbia. In fact, this is something that has been requested by them for some considerable time.
I realize, of course, that the minister has done a commendable piece of work in the carrying through of these negotiations. However, I should also like to give the fishermen themselves just a little bit of credit for this particular achievement. On May 11, 1955, I had the opportunity of participating in a debate with regard to fisheries problems. At that time I referred to a brief that had been sent to Mr. A. J. Whitmore, chief supervisor of fisheries, by one of the fisheries unions of British Columbia, and I gave this quotation as reported at page 3679 of Hansard, of that year:
Certain things stand out like a sore thumb. The Americans are getting 65 per cent of the Fraser pink catch, the Canadian fleet as a whole is getting about 35 per cent. Out of the total run, the fishermen in area 29D are getting about 1 per cent. Out of the Canadian portion, they are only getting about 3 per cent. Even out of the Fraser river area catch they only took about 12 per cent.
Fisheries
Yet it is suggested that closure of this area after September 16th would help solve the difficult problem of pink conservation.
As they submitted this brief, and in commenting on this particular situation, they suggested that one of the alternative proposals to the conservation methods that had been suggested by the minister would be the entering into of a treaty with the United States covering the conservation of the pink runs and the establishment of an equal catch. I just wanted to state that the fishermen themselves have been behind this proposition for some considerable time and that they and the minister, as interested parties working together, have been able to achieve this particular success.
I think the minister this afternoon stated that there was a time when the catch was in the ratio of 90 to 10 in favour of the United States fishermen. That ratio was gradually brought down until, as I have mentioned from a reading of this brief, it was at 65 per cent for the Americans and 35 per cent for the Canadians. So, as the situation developed and as the catch became more nearly equal, we find the United States fishermen and the United States authorities-or perhaps I should say the fishermen especially, in view of what the minister said this afternoon-had come to the place where they were more ready to accede to the request for the signing of a convention in this particular respect. I should like to say how much we appreciate the industry with which the minister pursued this objective. We are happy that the efforts have resulted in the achievement as indicated by this agreement.
My colleague the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn) has presented the case very well as far as we in this group are concerned. He raised the question as to the effectiveness or otherwise of the conservation measures which were instituted some time ago by the minister. Now, I am not going to discuss them except to say that there were two factors that were considered in this connection; one was conservation and the other was the quality of the fish that were taken. As I say, I am not going to enter into discussion of those factors, but I should like the minister to make it very clear when he closes the debate on this measure, whether or not he considers that the measures taken have resulted in the achievement of those objectives. I do not think the fishermen are convinced that is so. In fact, I am sure they do not think these measures have brought about the desired result. I should like the minister to make it very clear in this debate whether or not he and his officials consider these results

Fisheries
have been achieved, and also I should like him to submit what proof he has in this particular respect.
We are all agreed that the fishing industry is of vital importance to the economy of British Columbia, to Canada, and of course to the other nations who purchase fish from Canada. None of us has any desire to see the industry reduced or destroyed. There have been suggestions and a little interchange of views between my colleague the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn) and one or two of our friends in the C.C.F. group from British Columbia. I think I can assure them that the government of British Columbia is not contemplating any measure at all which will result in the destruction of this vital industry.
I have a clipping from the Vancouver Province of December 9, 1955. It is not new, but I think possibly it fits in about the same stage as some of these other references that have been made this evening. I quote the final paragraph from this report:
In Victoria, Premier Bennett reiterated Thursday that a proposal by the Moran Power Development Company to build a 700 foot hydro power dam on the Fraser, above Lillooet, won't be heard by the government until the fish problem has been resolved.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, I remember the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) himself saying on one occasion that the government of British Columbia was in full accord with the policy he held as regards this particular matter. I do not believe it is necessary for me to read tonight from the report of the fisheries association of British Columbia dated January 24, 1956. The Vancouver board of trade submitted a resolution to the provincial government which stated that the board endorsed the policies of the British Columbia government in regard to those matters having to do with power development on the Fraser and other rivers which are important to the fishing industry, and the report sets out quite clearly and positively that they support fully the views of the provincial government.
There has been a little bit of a play on words, Mr. Speaker. I have heard it today and also read it in the newspapers, fish or power and fish and power. I suppose it depends upon which way one looks at the situation. Perhaps a pessimist would take the view that it is fish versus power. I have some statements here which I could read, but I am not going to do that tonight, which present that point of view, that there is no possibility of getting to the place where we can have the fishing industry maintained if we are going to carry on power developments on these streams. On the other hand, the

optimist perhaps would take the other viewpoint that we trust that in the very near future the investigations and studies will reach a point where they are able to tell us that we can have a fishing industry and also the power developments on these particular streams.
Now, that is all I want to say at this time, Mr. Speaker, except to say that we do welcome the signing of this protocol and of course we will support the legislation which is now before us.

While I am not directly interested in commercial fishing and I am not one of the members of this group whose duty it is to deal particularly with fisheries affairs, I think, as a British Columbia member and one particularly interested iri the conservation of natural resources, I should like to make a few brief comments concerning this subject. I am sure we were all delighted with the minister's speech and his full explanation of this treaty this afternoon. I thoroughly enjoyed the speech made by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes). It was quite obvious he had done his homework before he started to speak. I would say the minister's speeches, and his obvious ability, act as a salve at times to heal the wounds caused by his occasional barbed comments iri this house. In any event, I must say I have been particularly pleased with his constructive approach to the problem of fisheries conservation on the Pacific and Atlantic in recent years. I am sure all of us in this group, all members in the house and particularly those from British Columbia, recognized the excellent work that has been done by the sockeye salmon fisheries commission, by the officials of his department and by the research workers iri the various other branches of the government. These ideas are not developed and these decisions are not reached without a great deal of work being done by people behind the scenes who often receive little recognition.
In view of what the minister had to say previously, I must also express my pleasure at the co-operative attitude on the part of the fishermen's union' in British Columbia. Apparently, they have been very concerned about this problem and have extended their co-operation in this respect to the minister and his department. However, I rose particularly to say, as a member who represents a riding that straddles the greatest area of the Columbia river in Canada, I was particularly pleased with the minister's explanation of the power or fish situation'. I was particularly pleased with his definition of his department's policy on this important

issue. It is one of great concern to the people of British Columbia. I want to express my whole-hearted support and the support of this group for the things he had to say with respect to the development of power and the conservation of our fishing industry in British Columbia. I was very happy indeed, because of the great concern to us in the interior, to hear him say that we should develop those rivers first in which fisheries are not involved before we start plans for rivers that will endanger our fishing industry. As a result of this policy, of course, the first development in British Columbia would naturally be the Mica creek dam north of Revelstoke. I have been extremely interested in this debate and I think it is of such great importance to the people of British Columbia that I intend to send a copy of today's Hansard to all the high schools, and other active organizations and to a great many other interested people in my district. I suggest it would be a good idea for British Columbia members generally to do something along that line so that the people who are interested in this vital question will have accurate information concerning the results of the efforts of the minister's department and will have the advantage of reading the minister's complete, thorough and specific explanation which he gave today.

Mr. Speaker, I think practically all of the subjects which could be raised in connection with this bill have already been thoroughly debated, but there is one point concerning which I would ask the minister to offer some clarification when he closes the debate.
In different parts of the bill-both in the operative part and in the schedule which, as the minister knows, consists of the convention between Canada and the United States and the protocol thereto-we find the expression "territorial waters". There is no definition of what is meant by those words. As the minister knows that has been a very difficult question on the west coast for many years. I am wondering how the term "territorial waters" is to be defined under this protocol to the convention and under this new bill.
For a good many years we have been urging that Canada adopt a 12-mile limit as her territorial waters. On the west coast, of course, we have also urged that the line be drawn from the tip of Vancouver island to the southern end of the Queen Charlotte islands and that Hecate strait be considered territorial waters, but that is not material in connection with this debate.
Fisheries
Some time ago a committee was appointed to investigate the whole question under Dean Curtis of the law faculty of the University of British Columbia. His report was submitted to the government in due course and last year in the house the Prime Minister told us that Canada intended to take the stand at the United Nations that she wanted her territorial waters to extend for 12 miles from her shorelines. I believe that stand was actually taken in the United Nations but no conclusion was reached and my own fear is that it will be a great many years before any decision can be reached in the United Nations on this question. Probably most of us here tonight will be in the Senate or in some other happy hunting ground before the United Nations gets around to any agreement. In the meantime because the territorial waters are an important part of the bill and the convention and protocol I hope the minister will explain just what is Canada's stand in connection with this measure in so far as territorial waters are concerned.

subtopic: SOCKEYE SALMON
subsubtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, needless to say I have been pleased and I know the officers of my department and the officers and scientists and members of the International Pacific Salmon Commission will be very gratified by the very warm praise which has been showered on them by members representing every party in this house for their very considerable achievements in the field of fisheries management.
If I could close this debate by turning to the points raised by individual members I shall commence with the remarks made by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes). The hon. member reminded us of the fact that last year as Minister of Fisheries I did refuse to have my departmental officers enforce a regulation proposed by the commission which I thought was in conflict with the treaty which had been approved by this house and I am glad to see that the hon. member thinks I was right in that action.
I did tell the commission that if they felt the power given to them was not wide enough to cover the situation which they were trying to handle then instead of trying to by-pass the convention they should ask us to amend the act, which we are now doing.
I may say that I was almost alone in this because the industry-and when I speak of the industry I am referring to the fishing operators and the fishermen-were hoping that there would not be fishing in the outside area that year because it was the year

Fisheries
of the small run and if they had some order to the effect that they should not fish there then they would be saved the expense of sending their boats that long distance. Since we share the catch equally, in the end it would not have increased the Canadian catch.
I was concerned, however, because to me it appeared to be a direct violation of the treaty which had been approved by this house which said that if part of the Canadian area was closed all the Canadian area had to be closed. It also seemed to me that this was going to weaken our efforts in having our fleet out there to out-fish the Americans on the pink salmon fishery. I thought it would be a poor precedent if this geographical advantage, which we have in having the outside fishery where the fish come first, was not to be exploited for even one year. One Canadian member of the commission heartily supported me in that contention.
Now that the pink salmon are included under this treaty this latter objection has of course disappeared. No matter whether we Canadians fish in the outside Canadian waters or the inside Canadian waters we are going to get half of the total catch of sockeye and pinks. It is more expensive to send our fleets to the outside waters since these fish in the end are going to turn up in the estuary of the Fraser river.
I realize that the fishermen of my hon. friend's riding find it more convenient to fish just off their shores as do the fishermen of my own riding, but one of the most attractive features of our modern new British Columbia fishing fleet is that it is extremely mobile. It ranges the whole coast of British Columbia and down off the coast of Washington and Oregon and up off the Alaskan panhandle. The only exception is this very privileged little fishery to which the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) referred, who have special rights above the Pattullo bridge, rights which have been measurably restricted in recent years; but I think now that we have the convention amended we can rest assured the Canadian members of the commission will see to it that the fishing effort is arranged to be of maximum advantage to the whole Canadian fishing fleet. We are going to get our full half share in any event.
The hon. member-I think with his tongue in his cheek-tried to lure me into discussing the proper division of catch between different types of gear. I know that the hon. member would never ask my colleague the Minister of Agriculture to decide how much wheat on the prairies should be cut by scythe and sickle, as it was earlier, or as it is now by binders and combines. That
[Mr. Sinclair.!	I
in effect is what sections of our fishing industry would like me as Minister of Fisheries to do. As Minister of Fisheries my job is to protect and conserve and if possible expand the fisheries of Canada. We do that by controlling the size of the fish caught, the size of the gear and the length of the season, but we are not going to arbitrate as between types of gear. We hope there will be the same natural evolution toward better and better and more efficient gear in our fisheries as there has been in every other form of Canadian industry.
There is another field in which the fishermen's unions have always been most anxious for me to intervene, and that is the matter of wages and prices. That again is not the responsibility of the Department of Fisheries, that is a process of collective bargaining under the provincial labour laws of British Columbia. I have resolutely refused to get into that division where a decision would be made whether the fish be caught by gill nets or seines, or to deal with price negotiations.
For the benefit of laymen in the house perhaps I should offer a word of explanation. The gill net is a curtain of net floated by floats on the top and weighted down by weights on the bottom, hanging in the sea and into which the fish stumble and are caught by the gills. It is an ambush, if you like. In the old days it could be used only at night because the fish could see the net in the day time, but with modern nylon nets which are almost invisible it can be used to catch fish by the gills in the day time as well as at night.
The seine is more of an ambush and trap. A school of fish detected, the ship runs around the school very quickly with a very deep net, the bottom of the net is pursed and the fish are trapped in the pursed seine. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes) pointed out a very interesting thing, the differentiation between the fishing industry and the example I used of the farming industry. We have gone from the scythe and the sickle to the binder and the combine, and the combine will still be on top. We are not going to revert because somebody has invented a way to make the sickle and the scythe more productive than the combine.
In fishing there has been a swing of the pendulum, which I think was the phrase used by my hon. friend. In the early days fishing on the west coast was done from skiffs. The canneries had tugs which each night would tow a long line of skiffs out to the fishing ground. These skiffs were powered only by oars. The men laid out their nets and in the morning the tugs picked them up and brought

them back to the cannery. That was the primitive beginning of gill netting. Then the boats got their own power and were able to go out by themselves.
Then the seiner came on the scene with bigger boats, more efficient boats and more powerful boats and it seemed as though the day of the gill netter was over. However, that is changing too because on our coast now we have big powerful gill net boats which range the whole coast from Oregon up to the Aleutian islands. The boats are well-manned and have efficient mechanical equipment. The net is put out and pulled in by great power drums. Actually today a good gill net boat on the west coast can go anywhere a seiner can go.
We brought in those fifteen deep-sea seiners when we were mounting this fishing offensive, if you might call it that. Today we find that a great number of gill netters are out there upon the Pacific. The gill netters are also beginning to move into another preserve of the seiners, the herring fishing which was almost entirely carried on by the seiners. Our department has been successful in developing a mid-water trawl, a small trawl which can fish at any level and which can pick up a ton or two of herring at a set. With these new large powerful gill netters which are very mobile and the mid-water trawls, we will see the gill netters moving into the herring fishery as well. These developments are brought about by the initiative of our progressive fishermen on the west coast. I certainly do not want to get into any position of deciding on the sort of gear that is going to be used to catch salmon.
A great deal of praise has been given to the Jones creek experiment where we and the B. C. Electric Company have made this artificial river. I do not want hon. members to be carried away with the idea that this is an answer to our problem. It seems to be a little bit of an answer to one of our problems, the problem of the pink salmon, but it is not an answer at all either to the problem of the sockeye salmon or the problem of the spring salmon. We have to do a great deal more work even on this project before we know whether it is going to be really successful with even the pink salmon.
The next project we are contemplating along this line is below the dam on the Cheakamus river in the Squamish valley which is likely to block out a pink salmon run completely. We are going to build a long artificial spawning bed below the dam there in order to create the very best conditions, the best water, the right depth and the
Fisheries
right sized gravel. If that is successful we will have taken quite a considerable stride forward in this matter of what might be called fish farming instead of fish trapping.
The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron), who is a bit of a scholar, expressed some surprise that a professor of geology at the University of British Columbia should suddenly become one of the leading fishing experts in Canada, if you can believe what you read in the press. I must confess that I have developed the same surprise. I know the gentleman very well, having been at engineering college and at Oxford with him. No doubt he is extremely well qualified in the field of geology but he knows no more about fishing than the average fisherman knows about geology. The trouble is that a lot of people who read his pronouncements on the Moran dam think he is speaking as a professor of fisheries because the University of British Columbia has the only institute of fisheries in Canada, an institute which has done good work in the field of fisheries. Many of their science professors have done excellent work over many years in fisheries research.
The hon. member spoke also of something I did not touch upon. Perhaps I was thinking too much in terms of the commercial value of our fisheries. He referred to the aesthetic and educational value of our fisheries. I do not suppose anyone who has ever seen this amazing return to the river, this surging, teeming silver horde pouring back as it has done for millions of years into the streams of British Columbia, who has seen the salmon spawning on our gravel beds, has not been moved by one of the real miracles of nature.
On my last trip to Vancouver I went out to see our new aquarium which was built in conjunction with the provincial government and the parks board in Vancouver. I am always amazed to watch not only the children but the adults as they examine this excellent display of fish in that aquarium. There is a fascination about fish even for people who will not eat fish. I hope we will cure that deficiency as the years go by.
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn) raised the matter of high seas fisheries and expressed the hope that we would ban them. Both the United States and Canada have already banned the high seas exploitation of salmon by the use of factory ships. It is true that the Japanese did use these methods, but they are on the Asian side of the ocean and are working on the Siberian fish. This is a problem which concerns the Russians and last year the Russians and the Japanese-I was going to say worked out

Fisheries
-signed a treaty; the Russians presented a treaty to them to sign. That is a problem affecting that side oi the ocean. We do not have that problem and we do not intend to have that problem because we feel that the fish are much better if we wait to catch them until they come to our shores when they can be handled quickly in shore plants.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) referred to the attitude of the British Columbia government on this matter of salmon streams. Nobody in public life in British Columbia has ever suggested that I am an admirer of the British Columbia government, but I have to pay them the tribute of saying that they did amend their local fisheries act which strengthened our hand in the matter of dealing with dams and other obstructions on salmon streams. I am aware of the statement made by Premier W. A. C. Bennett which was read by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) that he did not intend to grant any water rights for the construction of the Moran dam or other dams on the Fraser until such time as the Department of Fisheries had solved the problem of passing our salmon runs up and down over these dams.
The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) mentioned a problem which I had overlooked-the other important problem threatening the existence of salmon fishing in Washington, British Columbia and Alaska, too, for that matter. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) pointed out that all our good work in conservation could be ended if these great dams were allowed to be constructed. That is true, and I have told hon. members what we are trying to do to avoid that situation. But there is another development of the last year or two which is equally alarming-not high seas fishing, in the sense that we are going to have factory ships on the seas, with catcher boats picking up the fish, but what we call offshore fishing-fishing boats based in Washington or British Columbia or Alaska setting out from Canadian and American ports and going just beyond our territorial waters where they are outside ordinary control. There is the danger of such vessels laying miles of shallow nets in the open Pacific and intercepting the salmon before they come into our territorial or inland waters and rivers. We have two objections to that. The first is the economic point raised by the hon. member for Esqui-malt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes) the other evening when he asked: Why go to all the expense of sending big boats all that distance to catch fish and then have to transport them in refrigerators, when, if you will only wait,

the fish will find their way in to the river mouths where they can be caught more easily and transported in much better condition? Those who get out there first do, of course, reap a distinct advantage because they are getting in ahead of the other fishermen, but if this practice continues all the fishermen will eventually be out there fishing and all they will have done is to have placed an extra burden on fishing costs. That, however, is a minor reason why we oppose offshore fishing.
The major reason for opposing this type of fishing requires this explanation:	Hon.
members will remember that I spoke of the remarkable job which our scientists have done in identifying the various species of the five kinds of salmon as they come in. They have done even more than that. In this extraordinary Fraser watershed there are various races of fish, and each of the main tributaries of the Fraser, the south Thompson, the north Thompson, the Stewart, the Chilcoe, and a dozen others, has its own race of fish which goes in at different times a week or two apart.
In the earlier days when there was just an over-all closure, we lost entire races of fish because the fishing season was open long enough to wipe out a particular race which was going through at its peak at that time, but now our fishing closures are designed to treat each race of fish separately. In this way we shall get enough of the peak of each particular run through to its proper stream. But we can do that only as long as we have some control of the fish, and so long as they can be watched as they come round through Puget sound to the strait of Georgia. Naturally, we can exercise no such control when the fish are caught 100 miles out at sea and when we cannot distinguish one race from another or know when they intend to move in. The director of the International Pacific Salmon Fishing Commission has said that the scientists will lose control and effective management of each of the races in this watershed if this type of offshore fishing is permitted to continue.
This problem became acute last summer because of the increased mobility of these big gill-net boats which can now cover long distances and trail a mile of gillnet behind them. As Minister of Fisheries I can, under the Canadian Fisheries Act, stop Canadian fishermen from doing that tomorrow by order in council, because fishing in this country is a matter which is solely under the jurisdiction of the federal government. In the United States, however, authority over fisheries rests with the state governments and the federal government is unable to exercise

such control except in Alaska where they have banned offshore fishing. I have told our fishing industry, and I have told the American government, that I will not prevent Canadian fishermen doing this offshore fishing until such time as I know the Americans will ban similar American fishing, because we would be very foolish to stop our fishermen out there while leaving American fishermen to do that damage and get the benefit.
This weekend in Seattle the fishing authorities of the federal government of the United States, the states of Washington, Oregon and California, and our own deputy minister of fisheries are meeting with the regard to this problem which we all consider as an acute one, and we hope that the American state and federal governments will be able to come forward with a plan which will stop American fishermen from engaging in this offshore fishing. The day they come forward with that plan is the day we shall stop Canadian fishing of that type.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley raised once again this matter of the closure on the fishing for chum and pink salmon above Pattullo bridge. As I told the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn) a little earlier, it is true I made that closure, but I did so upon the advice of the scientists and advisers of my department who have done such a good job in managing the fisheries. I have explained this closure at great length to the fishermen's union and to the industry at various times. Happily, the responsibility for the closure so far as pink salmon are concerned will now be vested in the International Pacific Salmon Commission, and I think you will find the commission will be far stricter about that closure than I ever attempted to be.
The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) began very disarmingly and then mentioned that occasionally I made barbed remarks though not on fisheries questions. The hon. member might recall that if my remarks are barbed they are only so when the questions directed to me are barbed. I learned long ago in life that when people are nice to you it is easy to be nice to them, whereas when they are rough with you there is a temptation to be rough with them.
Certainly, everybody has been very kind now in this fisheries debate, so there was no occasion to be barbed. I am flattered that the hon. member is going to send a record of this debate to the high school children in his riding. I think it is very important that our children in British Columbia should learn more and more about this very unusual resource we have in the salmon industry-this 82715-112
Fisheries
very rich resource which, as I said earlier, is going to become more and more valuable as the years roll by. And they should appreciate, above all, that having such resources we should be intelligent enough to work out a policy by means of which we can have both fish and power. In view of the work already done by this International Pacific Salmon Commission in extending the sockeye fishery, we know they are going to do an equally good job in rebuilding the pink salmon industry, and if they can do that I believe it will be all the greater pity if a shortsighted policy because of the present demand for power should result in the end of this great resource.
Mr. Speaker, it is the intention to refer this bill now to the standing committee on fisheries at which I will have the director of the Pacific Salmon Commission and the other officers of my department available for questioning.

speechtext:
I am sorry, I did not pick up my last page. The hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra (Mr. Green) asked a very pertinent question about territorial waters. In both the bill and the protocol "waters" is defined as the waters of the high seas between the 48th and 49th parallel extending out to the 175th meridian, then the territorial waters of Canada and the United States and then, of course, the waters of the Fraser river itself. There is no definition given of territorial waters anywhere in the bill. That is given in other acts, both of congress and our parliament.
Whatever the territorial waters are, whether they are three miles out as they are now or 12 miles out as we hope they will be, this convention will apply. As far as the actual operation of the act is concerned, the definition of territorial waters is not too important because no matter where the catch is made on the high seas, in Canadian territorial waters or American territorial waters, it is going to be divided fifty-fifty between the Americans and the Canadians.
The hon. member was quite right in saying that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) had said that he had accepted the study made by the special law committee set up under Dean Curtis of U.B.C. and would recommend at the United Nations that our territorial waters be extended out to 12 miles to give us better control over the fisheries resources that we have been conserving. We did advocate that at the United Nations. We encountered very strong opposition from both the United Kingdom and the United States,

Fisheries
the two countries which are our closest triends, the two countries with which we have the greatest trade, even in fisheries products.
Both these countries felt very keenly that this move was not in their interests. That may be but I certainly know that the extension of the territorial waters of Canada from three miles from our shore to 12 miles from our shore on the base lines from headland to headland, which was approved by the international court of justice in the case of Norway against Britain, is something that our whole fishing industry wants.
As far as this legislation is concerned, no matter what the territorial limits are, three miles or 12 miles, the fish caught in that area are going to be divided equally between American and Canadian fishermen.

subtopic: SOCKEYE SALMON
subsubtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question? Would it not be possible for Canada to declare that she is adopting a 12 mile limit and then have a case taken to the international court of justice? If we got a favourable decision there, would we not have established definitely that our territorial waters extend out 12 miles?

subtopic: SOCKEYE SALMON
subsubtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I am not the best diplomat in the world. I have just been through these negotiations, if you want to call them that, with the Americans by which we got this treaty for the fish, so I am not averse to strong action provided you can see you have reasonable hope of success. But I am afraid that if we arbitrarily extended our limits to 12 miles we would find immediate retaliatory action taken against us by our principal customer, a customer which takes between 60 per cent and 70 per cent of our exports of fish. Fish is not like wheat. You cannot store fish on a farm or in a fisherman's house for two or three years or in elevators. When you have got it you have got to sell it.
It might well be we could take such a case to the international court and wait two or three years while the lawyers argued about it and we might win a great legal victory, but in that period we would have fish coming out of our noses-I was going to say coming out of our ears but coming out of our noses more than our ears-and a completely ruined fishing industry in Canada. The Prime Minister stated, I think, that our position is that there is no use in having an extension of territorial waters unless it is going to be accepted by the nations who claim historic rights, and more so on the east coast than on the west coast.

subtopic: SOCKEYE SALMON
subsubtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext: How far out do the Americans claim on the west coast?

subtopic: SOCKEYE SALMON
subsubtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext: Just three miles. The Americans have claimed title to the resources below the floor of the ocean out to the edge of the continental shelf. That is the Truman doctrine.

subtopic: SOCKEYE SALMON
subsubtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext: That is several hundred miles.

subtopic: SOCKEYE SALMON
subsubtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Sometimes the continental shelf is a mile off the shore. In the case of Newfoundland the continental shelf is 200 miles off the shore. That is what makes the continental shelf a very difficult boundary to accept in the fishing world because fishermen cannot tell where the continental shelf is below them. That is why a regular measured territorial zone from fixed base lines is much more understandable and enforceable from the point of view of the fishing industry.
We must remember that on the east coast, before there was any white settlement in Canada, there were European nations fishing for cod on the banks off Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. These nations, of course, assert that they have historic rights in these fisheries. I think that the majority of fishing nations of the world today believe firmly in the extension of territorial waters solely in the interests of conservation. At the conference of fishing nations in Rome two years ago the majority of the 55 nations there were certainly strongly in favour of it.
Among the six great fishing nations there is a pretty even division. Japan, the United States and the United Kingdom are what are called freedom of the seas nations. They want the territorial limits to remain at three miles so as to enable their fishing fleets to come as close to the shores of other nations as possible. Then there are what are called the coastal states, nations with great fisheries off their coasts which they want to conserve for their own nation, and of course they want to extend their territorial waters. These nations include Canada, Norway and Russia, the other three great fishing nations.
But as you get down to the smaller nations you find that they are almost all in favour of extension of territorial waters at least to 12 miles. Some of the South American nations have tried to establish their territorial waters 200 miles out.

subtopic: SOCKEYE SALMON
subsubtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
May I ask one question? When the minister referred to the difficulties which occurred last year over the suggestion by the commission that certain sections of our waters should be closed, he did not give assurance that there are safeguards in the new treaty to prevent the same difficulties arising again. When I spoke this afternoon I asked whether the amendment to article VI provided that safeguard which would prevent the possibility of the commission acting

as they intended to act last year, rather to the disadvantage of Canadian fishermen, by prohibiting fishing in Canadian waters. Now we have removed the provision stating that if prohibition is applied to any one section of waters it must apply to all similar waters.

subtopic: SOCKEYE SALMON
subsubtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I never questioned their
recommendation on the ground of its value to the fishing industry. I questioned it solely on the ground that it was beyond the scope of the treaty which had been approved by parliament and if they wanted a change they would have to come before us and explain why they wanted that change. They will be here when the bill is in committee. I had, of course, a second thought in my mind, that since we were conducting this campaign of fishing in outside Canadian waters for pinks and passing the Americans I certainly did not want to see any other type of fishing stopped in that area.
If the salmon commission can put forward a good reason, and I am sure they will be able to, for being given the right to open and close areas within the convention area in exactly the same fashion as our chief supervisor in Vancouver opens and closes areas over the entire British Columbia coast for the rest of the fisheries, then they should have that right. There is, of course, the safeguard by which an enforcement regulation now must secure the approval of the two governments. Under the earlier convention, once the commission had adopted regulations it was our duty and the duty of the state of Washington to use our enforcement staff to enforce them. We now intend to have concurrent approval by Washington and by ourselves before we do. But when Dr. Royal is before the committee he can pursue that matter further.

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour) moved
subtopic: INCREASED BENEFITS AND AMENDMENTS TO ADMINISTRATIVE PROVISIONS
INCREASED BENEFITS AND AMENDMENTS TO ADMINISTRATIVE PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the minister has said, this piece of legislation is merely to revise the rates of compensation payable to disabled seamen and their dependents. It perhaps could be a little bit better expressed by saying that it is merely designed to bring the amounts of compensation up to a level where they would be more in line with the compensation paid by the particular provinces. The legislation was first brought in with respect to this Merchant Seamen Compensation Act in 1946. I took the trouble to


look up the debate which took place at that time, Mr. Speaker. It was just after the war and there was a great deal of interest in our merchant seamen and the part which they played in helping to bring victory. They were getting more sympathy and they were more appreciated at that time. We recognized their effort. I remember reading how the then minister of transport, in introducing this legislation, paid great tribute to them and said that there were hopes for the future for our seamen and for our merchant navy in Canada. We know that those dreams have not been fulfilled for various reasons.
We now have a meagre merchant navy with very few trained seamen still following that line of endeavour. We do not know what our future is or where we are going. But I do say, Mr. Speaker, that the few seamen we do have left on the east and west coasts, and the ones who are affected by this act on the great lakes, certainly deserve the very best we can give them.
Naturally, when we see that the various rates are being increased we know that that is good. These seamen are deserving of that. This amendment will be the second amendment to the original act of 1946. When the bill goes to committee we shall still want to inquire into many aspects of this legislation. For example, we will want to know the number of accidents that have been considered and the number of refusals. There is one particular point I happened to notice in the explanatory note which I feel will need clarification. The explanatory note for subsection 6 of section 30 reads:
Formerly, the board had to decide how long compensation would be paid to an invalid child. The proposed subsection 6 provides that compensation in all cases will be paid to an invalid child until he ceases to be an invalid.
The obvious question there, Mr. Speaker, is who is to determine when the child is no longer an invalid? There is no mention of that in the bill.
There is just one other point I should like to mention into which we might inquire in the committee. I refer to the recent accidents in the piloting service which have been experienced in Halifax and Saint John. The house may recall that there was a serious accident in 1940 in Halifax. A few days ago in Saint John we had a pilot accident which concerned an incoming vessel and our No. 1 pilot boat. There were seven lives lost. The other day in the port of Halifax there was an accident concerning the aircraft carrier and a tugboat which resulted in the loss of two men. This brings forward

Merchant Seamen Compensation Act
the whole problem of pilot pensions which are now administered by their own fund. I understand there is some disagreement as to the future method which should be used. These pilots have a fund that would allow them a pension for dependents through the Department of Transport. Perhaps even more pertinently, Mr. Speaker, we might ask about the other men on these vessels. I think they are excluded from the act in some cases, but we should inquire into their situation and see that their families are being looked after in the way we should look after all our seamen.

subtopic: INCREASED BENEFITS AND AMENDMENTS TO ADMINISTRATIVE PROVISIONS
speechtext:
In
view of the fact this bill is going to the committee on industrial relations I am not going to make any detailed analysis of it. I am sure the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) and I will recognize that this bill is a long step forward in respect to seamen's compensation. Over the years he and I were the lone advocates in this house of a lot of things for the merchant seamen. In view of the fact we started with nothing, what we have before us represents a lot of progress in that time in this field.
While I was reading the bill it struck me that where the federal government has jurisdiction in matters of this kind they can bring about a lot of progress in a short time. If this had been a matter of dominion-provincial agreement like the national health insurance, and if we had started in 1946 by going to each province to get agreements about the differences that exist in rates, and tried to bring about uniformity in this kind of legislation, I am afraid we would still be waiting for that agreement. I make that observation because there is a lot of this type of legislation which I feel should be in the hands of a government that can enact it, and a government that has the finances to pay the bill.
Generally speaking, the rates in this bill are better than those obtaining in some of the provinces. It appears to me as though there was an attempt to bring about what would be an average if all the provinces were taken into consideration. So far as I am concerned, I am satisfied with the progress we have made in this type of compensation during the period we have been working upon it. No doubt when we go into committee we will be looking for a lot of information and clarification of the different clauses of the bill.

subtopic: INCREASED BENEFITS AND AMENDMENTS TO ADMINISTRATIVE PROVISIONS
speechtext:
I shall not take up too much time of the house in what I have to say on this matter. I do think this
is a step in the right direction, and it is one that is deserving of a good deal of consideration. I know that when the bill does go to the committee there will be a greater opportunity to ask more detailed questions of the minister, but it does seem to me it is a good thing in that it provides compensation for those seamen who are not now protected under provincial legislation. There will be some relationship between what compensation will be paid provincially and what will be paid federally. As other speakers have indicated, it is necessary that the seamen have some proper protection.
This is a step in the right direction, and apart from saying that the legislation is good in principle I think we all should wait until the bill reaches us and then we can have a more detailed study of it at that time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: INCREASED BENEFITS AND AMENDMENTS TO ADMINISTRATIVE PROVISIONS
speechtext:

speaks now, he will close the debate.

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: INCREASED BENEFITS AND AMENDMENTS TO ADMINISTRATIVE PROVISIONS
speechtext:
I should like to say a word, Mr. Speaker, and it will only take a moment. The hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) made a reference to a point about which I should like to add a word or two, particularly out of respect for his own service during the war. It was for me a special pleasure to work with my officials in drafting this legislation because of the fact that, even if they are now much fewer in number than we had hoped for, these seamen have upheld in peacetime the high tradition of service which they established during the war. I am glad on that account that this expression of the appreciation of that service will come into effect, judging by the endorsation the bill has received tonight.
The other point I wanted to mention was that we have given very full consideration to the matter of pilots and pilots' assistants. We have had discussions with the Department of Transport and the Department of Justice and when we go into committee I shall be prepared to deal with the subject. In the meantime, I have been assured that if anything can be done in that regard it can be done under regulation or order in council and it may not be necessary to make any amendments in the present legislation.

subtopic: TOXIC HAZARD PROTECTION
TOXIC HAZARD PROTECTION
subsubtopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
What assistance is being given by the Department of National Health and Welfare to agencies concerned with protecting industrial workers from toxic hazards of materials they are exposed to in their work?
Answer by: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
The occupational health division of the department has a highly trained group of physicians, chemists, engineers and physicists who, besides carrying out basic research on the health hazards of industry, on request assist provincial, federal and other agencies by surveying hazards caused by light, noise,
dust, vapours, fumes and gases in factories, mines, and other enterprises.
The most up to date equipment for analysing air samples is available. This includes such advanced equipment as the X-ray diffraction spectrometer, the electron microscope, infra-red and ultra-violet spectrometers and gas chromatography. When the hazard in the work situation has been evaluated, engineering staff recommends corrective measures.
Assistance is now being given toward solving the problem of arsenic occurring in connection with gold mining operations. A survey of fluorspar mines is also being carried on at the request of a province to assess the special hazards due to fluoride dust.
